problem: Existing embodied SocialNav policies (e.g. the iGibson 2021 challenge winner of Yokoyama et al.) are plain end-to-end RL PointNav policies that do not explicitly encode social properties such as proximity to humans, and SocialNav is evaluated only with coarse metrics (success, SPL, collisions).
motivation: A good social navigation policy must be safe as well as effective and efficient, so it must anticipate present and future collision danger with moving humans in occluded indoor spaces. Coarse aggregate metrics hide how agents behave in specific human-robot interactions, and questionnaire-based protocols do not scale to simulation test sets.
key_idea: Inject social awareness into an RL navigation policy through two privileged-supervision auxiliary tasks (Risk estimation and Proximity Compass) that predict near-term human proximity, and evaluate the policy with an automatic encounter-based protocol.
insight: Proximity auxiliary tasks improve success and reduce human collisions, and they are complementary to generic self-supervised tasks (CPC|A, GID): the combination gives the best results on both datasets (Gibson4+ SR 77.24 vs 72.65 baseline). The Compass task helps more on the larger HM3D-S scenes (Compass-only 67.32 SR vs Risk-only 66.22), and the self-supervised tasks smooth linear-velocity profiles in blind-corner encounters, whereas the baseline has to brake and backtrack. The encounter analysis shows that policies with similar coarse metrics differ in behaviour: Risk-only avoids encounters, while Compass-only accepts more encounters and survives them.
method: Policy architecture: ResNet-18 encoder for RGB-D (512-d) plus a linear GPS+Compass encoder (32-d), feeding a stack of parallel single-layer GRUs (512 hidden units each, following Ye et al.), each giving a 'belief'. A State Attention module fuses the beliefs into the mean and std of a Gaussian over (linear, angular) velocity. Trained with DD-PPO.

Risk Estimation task: an auxiliary regression target risk_t = clamp(1 - min distance to any person / D_r, 0, 1), predicted for the next k=4 steps from a belief and the action sequence. It captures imminent collision danger.

Proximity Compass task: the space around the agent is split into k angular sectors (north = heading), and the same clamped proximity value is computed per sector with a larger radius D_c > D_r. This gives long-range, weakly directional information about where people are.

Regressor networks: a single-layer GRU per task whose initial hidden state is the belief, fed with an embedding of future actions, and a linear output for the predicted proximity features. It is trained with an MSE auxiliary loss and is discarded at test time; GT proximity comes from simulator human positions only at training time.
Combination with self-supervised tasks: the proximity tasks are combined with 2 CPC|A tasks (2 and 4 steps) and GID (4 steps) from Ye et al., each on its own GRU belief.

Encounter-based evaluation protocol: encounters are extracted from trajectories with time, spatial and heading constraints and classified with inclusion rules into frontal, intersection, blind corner and person following. Metrics are Encounter Survival Rate, Average Linear Velocity and Average Distance.
HM3D-S dataset: social navigation episodes on 900 HM3D scenes (8M train, 450 val, 490 test episodes) with pedestrians walking back and forth along shortest paths at 0.45-0.5 m/s.

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 visual encoder + parallel GRU beliefs with state attention (trained from scratch with DD-PPO)
setting.training_data: Gibson4+ (64 train scenes, ~100M steps), then fine-tuned on HM3D-S (800 scenes, 8M episodes, ~40M steps); RL with auxiliary losses; no extra web data
setting.action_space: continuous velocity (normalized linear and angular velocity in [-1,1]), stop within 0.2 m of goal, 500-step budget
setting.privileged: GT human positions from the simulator used only as training-time auxiliary targets; none at test time

results: The full model (Proximity + Aux tasks) reaches 77.24 SR / 55.23 SPL / 19.50 human-collision rate on Gibson4+ and 70.16 / 47.60 / 22.09 on HM3D-S. It beats the Yokoyama et al. baseline (72.65 SR / 47.43 SPL / 24.35 H-Col on Gibson4+) and the aux-only baseline (73.4 SR / 52.08 SPL). The fine-grained analysis shows behaviour differences hidden by the coarse metrics.
limitations: Simulated humans are simplistic (constant-speed back-and-forth walking, no natural animation or social cues), so the learned behaviour may not transfer to real crowds; no sim2real experiments.
Proximity targets need GT human positions at training time, and the encounter classification uses hand-set heuristic thresholds.
Gains are modest and standard deviations are large (about 1-2 points), so some ablation differences are within noise; RGB helps on Gibson4+ but not on HM3D-S.
